column1: # Player-facing settings: the iOS launcher (dm/ios/Sources/Launcher.swift) and the Mac app's settings window (dm/mac/Launcher.swift) show them before the game starts; Mac front ends read the same list.

# dm/games/settings.py writes one game's list into its app (dm/launcher.json; build_ipa.sh, and dm/mac/pack_app.py through the NSP script): the rows whose condition holds for that game, with its defaults. Each sets an environment variable the host reads when the game starts; one an env file sets
# (Documents/env.txt, the bundle's dm/env.txt) is shown but kept. Diagnostic switches stay environment-only, so they are not listed here. The player's page is docs/settings.md.
#   variable  the environment variable the setting sets

#   kind      choice: values value=label,..., an option only some games have with ?<shown>&<shown> after its label (languages: the game's own, from its control data; every language when it has none, with a note); range: values low:high:step, shown as a percentage;
#             toggle: values - (on sets 1, off 0) or <on>/<off>, the two values the variable takes (on/off)
#   default   a value (a toggle's: 1 on, 0 off); DM_GAME_<NAME>: the host's own default from the game profile (game_profile.h, game.py); build:<VAR>: the IPA build's setting (build_ipa.sh)
#             <ios>|<mac> selects the platform's default before resolving a profile macro or build variable

#   shown     always; DM_GAME_<NAME>!=<value> or ==<value>; fixups:<KEY>: main's rewriter table has that key (a stub in the game's build, patch_nso.py); languages>1 (more than one to pick, so also when the control data lists none); gfxapi:<API>: the packer's GFXAPI;
#             platform:<ios | mac>: the app's platform (SETTINGS_PLATFORM, ios when unset), for a switch only that platform's front end reads
#   section   the settings screen's tab the row is on: one of settings.py TABS (Game, Picture, Smoothness, Controls, Performance, Diagnostics), which also gives each tab's icon and
#             its two descriptions. Tabs come in TABS order; rows appear in table order within each tab. Reset to tested defaults clears all launcher choices; values fixed by an env file stay

#   label, note  the setting's name and the line under it (may be empty), in plain words anyone can follow: what it does for the player, its cost (latency, memory, heat, battery), then the setting recommended, as "Recommended: ..."
#   tech      optional: the technical description, shown when the player asks for technical details: how the host does it, the measurements behind the recommendation
#   meta      optional, key=value pairs separated by ; (settings.py META lists the keys; docs/frontends.md, The settings list, describes them):
#             level=basic  a setting a front end shows first;  needs=<VAR>=<value>  a sub-setting, drawn only while the row that sets <VAR> has that value

column8: The language of the game's menus, text and voices.
column9: The system language the host reports to the game, in place of the one the app was packed with. The list comes from the game's control data (NACP).

column8: Plays as if the Switch were on a TV (Docked) or in your hands (Handheld). Handheld is lighter and cooler on a phone. Recommended: Handheld on an iPhone.
column9: The operation mode the host reports to the game, which picks its render resolution and performance mode. Docked renders at the TV resolution: heavier and warmer, and little sharper on a phone screen.

column8: Play in a window or on the whole screen.
column9: Whether the game window opens in macOS full screen. It can still be changed while the game runs.

column8: Normal is the game's usual sharpness. Potato is a lighter mode, for 60 fps on a warm phone. Recommended: Normal.
column9: Normal renders 1280×720 handheld (1951×1098 docked), steady at 30 fps. Potato is the game's lighter mode: 960×540 shown at 720p.

column8: How sharp the 3D world is drawn. Lower is blurrier but much lighter on the phone; menus and text stay sharp. Recommended: 0.60 on an iPhone. Lower it first if frames drop in busy areas.
column9: Scales the game's 3D render targets from their size in the selected console mode. Below 100% the size is fixed and the game's dynamic resolution is off; the HUD is drawn at full size. It is the setting that frees the most GPU time.

column8: Lets the game lower its sharpness by itself when a scene gets busy. Off keeps it sharp all the time. Recommended: off when you set a Render scale.
column9: The game's own dynamic resolution, which scales its 3D views between 70% and 100% under GPU load. Off, a patch in the game's code holds them at the full size of the selected console mode.

column8: How the game's picture is enlarged to fill your screen. MetalFX looks sharper but uses more battery and heat. Recommended: Standard.
column9: Scales the finished frame, HUD included, to the screen: Standard is smooth (linear) scaling, MetalFX is Apple's spatial upscaler. Nothing changes while the frame is already the screen's size; devices without MetalFX use Standard.

column8: Some games enlarge their own picture in a heavy way. MetalFX does the same job much faster, with Apple's look instead of the game's. Recommended: MetalFX.
column9: Replaces the game's own upscaling network (agl's NDSR) inside the frame with the MetalFX spatial scaler, at the same input and output sizes: about 1 ms where the game's takes several (3.5-5 ms on an M1).

column8: Fit shows the whole picture, with black bars. Fill covers the whole screen and cuts off the edges, where health bars, subtitles or maps can be. Recommended: Fit.
column9: Fill scales the 16:9 frame until it covers the screen and crops what lies outside; nothing is stretched. It applies in landscape; portrait and a TV always fit. A full-screen picture without cropping needs a patch for each game (Wide view).

column8: Fills the whole iPhone screen with a wider view of the world and no black bars. A little slower and warmer; takes effect the next time the game starts. Recommended: off with Frame generation, on for 30 fps without it.
column9: A patch in the game widens its camera and renders the 3D views at the screen's shape: about a fifth more pixels, and more memory for the render targets.

column8: Draws a taller picture that matches the iPhone Duo's screen. A little slower and warmer.
column9: Renders at 1.43:1 instead of 16:9: the sides of 16:9 with more above and below, and the HUD at the screen's edges. About a quarter more pixels.

column8: How many pictures a second the game shows. More is smoother, but uses more battery and heat. Recommended: 30 fps with Frame generation on; 60 fps heats an iPhone within a few minutes, and iOS then slows it down.
column9: The host paces the game's frame loop to this rate, at the game's real speed. 120 fps (Mac) needs a 120 Hz display; when frames do not fit, the game drops to 60 for a while.

column8: Makes the game look like 60 fps while it works at 30: a made-up picture is shown between each two real ones. Cooler than real 60, but the controls answer a little later and fast motion can smear. Recommended: on.
column9: MetalFX frame interpolation (iOS 26 / macOS 26): between two game frames it builds the halfway one from the game's depth and the motion it estimates, with the HUD kept out. Each real frame waits about half a frame (17 ms). It backs off to the game's own frames while frames drop. Works best with Deadline boost, Real-time presenting and Encode thread on.

column8: Lighter makes the in-between pictures a little smaller to save work; the picture looks slightly softer. Recommended: Full; Lighter if frames drop in busy areas.
column9: Lighter interpolates at 0.75 of the picture's size and MetalFX scales the result back up: about half of frame generation's GPU time, the HUD softened too.

column8: Lets the game start its next picture before the screen has finished with the last one: steadier, with up to one frame more latency on the controls. Recommended: on. Frame generation turns it on anyway.
column9: Each finished frame is copied into a two-image buffer the screen shows from, so the game's image is free at once and the GPU never idles (iOS would read idle time as spare and lower its clock). Costs up to one frame of latency (about 28 ms on an iPhone 17 Pro Max) and two frame-sized images.

column8: When the game cannot keep up, it drops to an even, lower frame rate for a while instead of jumping between two. Recommended: off at a fixed 30 fps.
column9: After 3 late frames in a row, each frame is held for one more refresh (60 to 30 fps) until frames fit again. Off, a late frame is shown one refresh later and the next goes on as usual.

column8: A light tap from the phone when you press an on-screen button.
column9: A haptic impact from the Taptic Engine for each on-screen gamepad button press.

column8: The colours of the on-screen buttons.
column9: The on-screen gamepad's theme; the game's profile picks its default.

column8: Lets the game vibrate the phone or your controller.
column9: Passes the vibration values the game sends through hid to the phone's haptics or to a connected controller's motors.

column8: How strong the vibration is, from none to three times the game's.
column9: A gain of 0 to 300% on the vibration amplitude the game sends, limited at the motors' maximum.

column8: Stops a weak, constant buzz on some controllers: vibration weaker than this stays off.
column9: Amplitudes below the cutoff are dropped and the rest is spread over the full range; the phone's own vibration is not affected. A controller with rotating motors in Mario Kart 8 Deluxe needs about 45%.

column8: For iPhones with less memory (8 GB, such as the iPhone 15 Pro): makes the game use less memory so it does not close. Recommended: off, unless the game closes on an 8 GB iPhone.
column9: DM_PRESET=potato turns on this game's memory savers, a list of settings from its profile; the rows it sets are locked while it is on. Off, none of them runs.

column8: Asks iOS to keep the game on the phone's fast cores. Uses more battery and heat. Recommended: on. Off, a warm phone moves the game to the slow cores and frames drop.
column9: The threads that make a frame (acquire, encode, command-buffer recording) join one os_workgroup with each frame's deadline, so the scheduler keeps them on the performance cores at a higher clock.

column8: Keeps the helper that shows each picture on time. Off may use a little less battery, with a risk of more stutter. Recommended: on.
column9: Gives the present thread a time-constraint (real-time) scheduling policy for the share of each frame it needs; off, it has a QoS class only.

column8: Prepares each picture's graphics work on a helper of its own, so the game does not wait for it. Recommended: on. Off, frames come late, with stutter.
column9: Translates the game's NVN command buffers into Metal commands on a thread of its own instead of the game's submitting thread (about 4 ms a frame instead of 8 in Breath of the Wild). Frame buffering needs it for games that present from another thread.

column8: Remembers the graphics the game has drawn, so new areas stutter less. Uses more memory. Recommended: on.
column9: Keeps a Metal 4 pipeline archive and builds most pipelines in microseconds from a shared base. A pipeline never seen draws with a hybrid stand-in for its shader pair while the real one is built in the background.

column8: Prepares all of the game's graphics in advance, for fewer stutters later. The first start waits a few minutes for it, once. Recommended: on.
column9: Builds a stand-in pipeline for every shader pair the game has (15,767 for Breath of the Wild) into the archive, behind a Preparing pipelines screen; again after a game or app update that brings new shaders.

column8: Skips drawing things the game found hidden, to save work. Something coming into view can appear a moment late. Recommended: off; try it if frames drop in busy areas.
column9: Conditional rendering: a condition whose samples-passed query has not landed yet takes the previous result instead of drawing. Saves GPU time; an object coming into view can be drawn a frame late.

column8: Shows in a corner how many pictures a second you get. Recommended: off; turn it on to check the frame rate.
column9: The front end's count of presented frames per second. On the Mac it also shows the longest frame of the last second and the GPU time per frame.

column8: Apple's overlay with frame times and memory, to see how the game runs. Costs a little GPU time. Recommended: off; on only to measure.
column9: The Metal Performance HUD (MTL_HUD_ENABLED, set before the first Metal device): frame rate, frame and GPU times, memory.
